### On Learning How to Notice

There is a moment, just after you wake up but before you remember who you are supposed to be for the day, when the world is oddly simple. Light comes through the blinds in clean lines. The air in the room has a temperature and a weight. Somewhere outside, a bus brakes - that soft hydraulic sigh - and a bird that you have never learned the name of starts working on the same three notes over and over again, as if it is trying to get them right.

Most of us miss that moment completely. We reach for our phones. We remember the email we forgot to send, the conversation we replayed too many times last night, the small ache in our shoulder. The day assembles itself very quickly, like scaffolding clicking into place around that quiet little half-minute.

I’ve been trying, for the past few years, to stay in that half-minute a little longer. Not in a meditative, incense-and-chanting way — although I respect people who can do that — but in a more stubborn, almost childish way. To notice things.

Noticing sounds easy until you try to do it on purpose.

Take your kitchen. You’ve seen it a thousand times. You know where the mug with the chipped handle lives, you know which drawer sticks if you pull it too fast, you know the faint discoloration on the ceiling from when the upstairs neighbor’s plant watering got ambitious. You navigate it blind, half-asleep. You think you know it.

Now try to describe it to someone who has never seen it. Not the layout — the *details*. The way the light hits the faucet at 4 p.m. and makes a bright coin on the backsplash. The sound the refrigerator makes right before its motor kicks in, that tiny tick like it’s clearing its throat. The weird way your cutting board has warped just enough that it rocks slightly if you press on the corner. The collection of magnets on the fridge that have no business being together but somehow are: a souvenir from a beach town you barely remember, an emergency dentist’s number, a child’s drawing of a dog that looks more like a horse, a postcard you kept because the blue on it was exactly the right blue.

You realize how much you look at without seeing. We live in a state of highly efficient blindness. Our brains are wonderful editors. They cut out 99% of the sensory footage because otherwise we’d never get anything done. If you actually perceived every texture, every shadow, every ambient sound simultaneously, you would be overwhelmed and useless, frozen in the doorway like a tourist in your own life.

But the trade-off is that we miss a lot of beauty by being so efficient. And not just beauty — we miss information. We miss cues about how we’re actually feeling.

I learned this the embarrassing way. A few years ago I went through a stretch where I was busy in that modern, badge-of-honor way: too many projects, too little sleep, saying yes to everything because saying yes feels like being loved. I told everyone I was fine. And I believed it, because my narrative brain — the efficient editor — kept writing the headline: FINE. FUNCTIONING. ON SCHEDULE.

My body knew better. It was keeping a different ledger. My jaw was tight all the time. I was getting headaches at 3 p.m. every day, right behind the eyes. I stopped wanting to go for walks, which for me is like a canary in the coal mine. I like walks. I *am* a person who goes for walks. When I don’t, something is off. But I didn’t notice until a friend asked me, very casually over coffee, “When was the last time you went to the park just to go? Not to get somewhere, just to sit?”

I had no answer. I couldn’t remember.

That question cracked something open. I started walking again, not for exercise, not with a podcast filling my ears to optimize the time, but just to walk. At first it felt indulgent, even wasteful. Ten minutes. Twenty. Around the block with no destination. I noticed how stupid it felt, which is itself worth noticing.

And then I started noticing other things, because when you give your brain a little less to do, it starts to offer things back.

I noticed that my neighborhood has an astonishing number of different fences. Wooden ones gone silver with age. Chain-link ones with plastic vines threaded through in a hopeful gesture toward privacy. A low brick wall that someone clearly built by hand, the mortar a little wobbly, a tiny unevenness that made me like it immediately. I noticed that the old woman three doors down always sweeps her porch at the same time every morning, not quickly, but with care, like she is tending something. I noticed that the tree on the corner, which I had always thought was one tree, is actually two trees braided together, fighting and holding each other up at the same time.

None of this is important. That’s the point. It’s unimportant in the way that air is unimportant until you think about it.

We live in an age that wants everything to be important, measurable, productive. Hobbies must become side hustles. Walks must be 10,000 steps. Reading must be a reading challenge. Even rest has been turned into a performance: sleep scores, recovery metrics, mindfulness streaks. We’ve taken the unquantifiable parts of being alive and tried to put numbers on them so we can grade ourselves.

Noticing is the opposite of that. It doesn’t accumulate. It doesn’t build toward anything. You can’t put it on a resume. You will not get better at noticing in a way that makes you rich or famous, and if you try to gamify it — “I noticed 57 things today!” — you ruin it completely, like trying to be extra spontaneous at 2 p.m. on Tuesday.

It’s a quieter skill. It’s standing at a window while it rains and actually watching the rain, how it doesn’t fall straight but is pulled and pushed by air you can’t see. It’s listening to a friend talk and hearing not just the story but the way their voice changes when they get to the part that still hurts. It’s catching yourself mid-scroll, thumb hovering over infinite content, and asking — gently, without judgment — “What am I looking for right now? What do I actually want?”

Often the answer is: I want to feel less lonely. Or less anxious. Or just less blah. And somehow, the act of asking is more soothing than whatever answer the feed was going to give you.

I think we’re hungry for permission to pay attention slowly. The world is so fast and so loud. Everything is breaking news, trending, urgent. If we don’t keep up, we feel we will be left behind, uninformed, irrelevant. So we skim. We scan headlines. We watch videos at double speed. We pride ourselves on getting the gist.

But the gist is not the thing. The gist is the husk of the thing.

The thing itself is always slower, more detailed, more contradictory. A person is not their opinion about politics. A city is not its reputation. A book is not its summary. A day is not the three bullet points you write in your journal at night to prove you lived it.

I keep a little notebook now. Not a fancy one, and not consistently — I’m not trying to add a new chore to my life. But sometimes, when I’m waiting for the kettle to boil or sitting on the train, I write down one weirdly specific thing I saw that day. No analysis. No moral. Just:

*The grocer stacked the oranges in a perfect pyramid and stepped back to look at it for a second, proud.*

*Pigeon with only one foot, still strutting like it owns the sidewalk.*

*The way my friend laughed so hard she snorted and then immediately pretended she hadn’t.*

On bad days, I flip through it. It doesn’t fix anything. It doesn’t tell me what to do about money or mortality or the larger sadnesses of the world. What it does is remind me that I was there. That even on the worst days, I was still in the world, and the world was still there, offering these tiny, ridiculous, tender details for free.

And maybe that’s enough of a purpose for any of us: to be here while we’re here, and to notice it.

Not to master it, not to capture it perfectly, not to turn it into content. Just to see it clearly while we can. To let the light fall on the faucet at 4 p.m. and make that bright coin, and to be awake for it this time.

Tomorrow, the light will hit a little differently. Tomorrow, the bird will try those three notes again. Tomorrow, my shoulder might not ache, or it might. Either way, there will be something to notice, if I’m willing to waste a little time doing it.

I hope I am.
